CSS Virginia. The Confederate ironclad built from the salvaged hull of the Union frigate USS Merrimack, she devastated Union wooden warships at the Battle of Hampton Roads until checked by the Union ironclad USS Monitor. Though not ultimately a strategic success for the Confederacy, her engagement with Monitor fundamentally transformed naval warfare.

The Virginia was constructed by the Confederacy from the burned hull of USS Merrimack, a Union steam frigate scuttled in Norfolk harbor, with armor plating built from railroad iron over wooden backing. On March 8, 1862, she attacked the Union blockade fleet at Hampton Roads, destroying the wooden frigate USS Cumberland and the sloop USS Congress in a shocking display of ironclad superiority. The next day, March 9, she engaged USS Monitor in a historic duel that lasted four hours, with neither ship able to decisively damage the other, ending her dominance of the roadstead.

Withdrawn by Confederate forces, Virginia was eventually scuttled in May 1862 when Union forces captured Norfolk, denying her to the enemy. Her maiden action proved that ironclad warships could overwhelm traditional wooden navies, accelerating armament races worldwide. The combined Hampton Roads engagement marks the definitive end of the wooden warship era in naval history. She was the Confederacy's boldest technological gambit for naval parity with the Union and remains the most famous and destructive vessel in the Southern fleet.
